summary: Rare diseases each affect fewer than 200,000 people in the U.S., but there are thousands of them, and most have no approved treatment. Many are caused by a single faulty gene, which makes them natural targets for gene therapy, RNA drugs and enzyme replacement. Small patient numbers are offset by orphan-drug incentives, faster regulatory paths and high prices.

sections.heading: Main approaches
sections.body:
• Gene therapy uses a harmless virus (usually AAV) to deliver a working copy of a gene, often as a one-time treatment. Duchenne muscular dystrophy, hemophilia and Huntington's disease are active areas.
  • RNA drugs, including antisense oligonucleotides and siRNA, raise or lower production of a specific protein. Newer versions are linked to antibodies to reach muscle or brain.
  • Enzyme replacement and small molecules supply a missing enzyme, help a misfolded protein work, or block the harmful product of a disease pathway.

sections.heading: Why the economics differ
sections.body: Orphan drug designation brings seven years of U.S. market exclusivity and tax credits. Priority review vouchers, which can be sold for around $100M or more, add to the incentives. Trials are small and often use accelerated approval based on a biomarker. That speeds approval, but confirmatory trials can fail and force a drug off the market. Gene therapies have also run into safety problems, including liver toxicity and deaths, which have led to label restrictions and clinical holds.

sections.heading: What investors watch
sections.body:
• Biomarker vs functional results: whether the protein increase or biomarker change translates into better strength, survival or quality of life.
  • Launch metrics: patients identified, time to treatment and payer coverage. Rare-disease launches are slow and lumpy.
  • Safety across larger groups, especially for gene therapies given to older or sicker patients.
  • Manufacturing: viral vector supply and cost, which can cap the number of patients treated.
